title: Saudi Aramco Cuts Europe Off From October Crude as Macron Seeks Emergency Stock Release; Record Diesel and TTF Prices Push G7 Toward Action
subhead: Saudi Aramco told European term buyers they will receive no crude in October after the East-West pipeline outage, rerouting roughly 60 million barrels through Hormuz to Asian refiners instead. With Europe's diesel benchmark above $200 a barrel, Macron is calling the G7 back to the table for another emergency stock release while EU gas storage sits at two-decade lows.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Cuts Europe to Zero on October Crude as Pipeline Workaround Skips the Continent
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco has told European term customers they will receive no Saudi crude in October, with at least two European refiners informed their October allocations are zero and people familiar with the decision saying it applies to all European term buyers, Bloomberg reported via OilPrice.com. The move follows the shutdown of the kingdom's East-West pipeline — which carried 4-5 million barrels per day across Arabia to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing Hormuz — after drone attacks launched from Iraqi territory near the Iranian border.

Rather than supply Europe, Aramco has sold about 60 million barrels from its Persian Gulf terminal at Ras Tanura for September-October loading, moving them through Hormuz and via ship-to-ship transfers at Sohar, Oman, per Reuters. That program restores roughly 1-1.5 million bpd of Saudi Gulf exports, but the buyers are in China, South Korea, India and Japan — decidedly not Europe. Dated Brent, the physical European benchmark, topped $130 this week, while Poland's Orlen is scrambling for North Sea, US and Kazakh barrels after Saudi September cargoes were delayed or canceled.
sections.whyItMatters: The geographic split in Saudi export recovery is stark: Asia gets the crude that once bypassed Hormuz, while Europe — whose refiners relied on the Yanbu-SUMED route — is cut off entirely. It reveals how a chokepoint war reorders who gets energy, with the Atlantic basin losing access even as Gulf oil flows partially resume.

sections.heading: Macron Calls for Another Emergency Oil Release as Europe's Diesel Crisis Deepens
sections.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron said Friday he will convene G7 countries in the coming weeks to coordinate stock levels, exports and production capacity and consider tapping strategic reserves, as Europe loses Saudi crude and diesel prices push deeper into record territory, OilPrice.com reports. Paris is also working to secure diesel, jet fuel and natural gas supplies for the coming months.

The pain is concentrated in diesel. Europe's diesel benchmark rose to more than $200 per barrel this week, with taxes pushing retail-equivalent costs above $300. Russia has extended restrictions on diesel exports, and Middle Eastern product exports remain constrained. European emergency stocks — unlike the US SPR — hold large volumes of finished fuels including gasoline and diesel, giving the bloc a card it can play directly on the product market. IEA members have already released more than 300 million barrels of emergency stocks since March, and global observed inventories sit 507 million barrels below where they were when the war began.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is being forced to burn its strategic stockpile on products, not just crude, and the G7 has largely exhausted the stock-release lever. The shift signals that the continent is now managing an acute end-use fuel crunch — diesel and jet fuel — that pipeline repairs, stock releases and alternate crude sourcing cannot quickly solve.

sections.heading: Oil Heads for Weekly Loss as Saudi Export Fears Ease, but Benchmarks Stay Elevated
sections.body:
Oil prices were set for a weekly decline after three weeks of gains as fears that Saudi Arabia could not keep exporting eased on reports of the ship-to-ship transfers, Reuters and OilPrice.com report. On Friday, Brent traded around $103.90 (down roughly 0.9%) and WTI near $99.40 (down about 2.5%), well below Brent's intraday push above $108 earlier in the week. Murban futures, a Gulf benchmark, were at about $117.90.

The US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Tuesday crude should flow through the East-West pipeline 'within days'; Aramco is targeting a return of about half capacity within days, but full recovery is unlikely for another six weeks. The market had spent days staring at 4-5 million bpd potentially stranded behind the damaged pipeline before Aramco's Oman workaround partially relieved the squeeze.
sections.whyItMatters: The weekly fall shows the market's worst-case supply fears have been priced back, but the relief is partial — oil still holds above $100 and the physical premium (Dated Brent near $130) is far steeper than the futures curve suggests, because rerouting Gulf barrels to Asia has not helped the Atlantic basin.

sections.heading: LNG Cargoes Begin Pushing Through Hormuz as Qatar and UAE Test the Chokepoint
sections.body:
At least two LNG carriers have transited the Strait of Hormuz this week, while two others were detected in ship-to-ship transfers offshore Oman, according to tanker-tracking and satellite data compiled by Bloomberg. The uptick signals that Gulf LNG exporters — mostly Qatar and the UAE — are intensifying efforts to push supply through the chokepoint after months of near-total halt, OilPrice.com reports.

Unlike crude, LNG is far harder to shuttle-ship and reload via STS transfers, yet at least three STS transfers of LNG cargoes offshore Oman have been spotted over the past month. In pre-war times, three LNG cargoes per day exited Hormuz. The choked flows have kept gas prices at their highest since the 2022-2023 crisis, with Northeast Asian spot LNG at $28.40 per MMBtu this week and TTF at $92.95 (80.5 euros per MWh), up slightly on Wednesday after five straight weeks of gains.
sections.whyItMatters: The restart of LNG transit through Hormuz — even in trickles — is the first real sign Gulf gas producers are adapting to the blockade using the same STS playbook oil has used. But volumes remain a fraction of pre-war, and the winter competition between Europe and Asia for non-Hormuz cargoes keeps prices structurally tight.

sections.heading: Germany Confronts a Record-Low Gas Storage Crunch With Just Weeks Before Winter
sections.body:
Germany, Europe's biggest economy and the owner of the world's fourth-largest gas storage capacity, is weighing an expanded market incentive to lift storage levels after sites stood only 56% full in mid-September — the lowest in at least a decade and a half, per Gas Infrastructure Europe data cited by Reuters. The government is considering scaling up its autumn tender for Long Term Options (LTOs) to encourage traders to hold gas for later delivery, and has agreed with state-held firms Uniper and SEFE to inject more gas into their facilities.

The problem is structural: soaring gas prices have deepened backwardation, making it uneconomical for traders to store gas for winter. Industry body INES warns the 'window for sufficient refill is closing' and that Germany risks shortages if the winter is colder than average. ING strategists note Europe will 'struggle to hit its lower storage target of 75% ahead of winter' even as JKM-TTF spreads signal the region should be pulling in spot cargoes.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany's storage shortfall is the EU's single biggest winter risk — the country alone holds a quarter of the bloc's capacity. Its move to pay traders to refill rather than buy gas directly, as in 2022, is a market-based adaptation to an energy security emergency, but 56% full with weeks to go leaves little margin against a cold spell.

sections.heading: TotalEnergies and BlackRock Strike $1.8 Billion Deal on African Oil and Gas Infrastructure
sections.body:
TotalEnergies and BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) signed a partnership under which GIP will invest $1.8 billion in the French supermajor's oil and gas infrastructure assets in Africa, TotalEnergies announced Friday and OilPrice.com reported. In exchange for the capital contribution, TotalEnergies will pay GIP a tariff over up to 15 years, based on the assets' throughput. The companies did not specify which assets are covered.

The deal extends TotalEnergies' deepening push into Africa amid the global supply squeeze — it recently brought its Acacia-5 discovery in Angola toward first oil just months after discovery, expanded offshore Namibia's Mopane and Venus discoveries, and, with China's CNOOC, is developing the Tilenga and Kingfisher fields in Uganda that will make the landlocked country the world's newest crude exporter in early 2027 via the $5 billion East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) to Tanzania's port of Tanga.
sections.whyItMatters: As Gulf and Russian supply routes stay disrupted, Western capital is being redeployed into non-chokepoint African supply — Angola, Namibia and Uganda — that can reach markets without Hormuz or the Red Sea. The BlackRock-GIP partnership signals infrastructure investors treating African midstream as a strategic hedge against instability in established transit corridors.

bottomLine: The day's dominant development is a redrawing of who gets energy in a chokepoint war: Saudi Aramco has effectively cut Europe out of October supply, pushing 60 million barrels through Hormuz to Asian buyers instead, while France calls for another G7 emergency stock release as Europe's diesel benchmark breaks $200. Crude eased on relief that Saudi exports are still flowing via Oman ship-to-ship transfers, but the physical squeeze remains — Dated Brent near $130, TTF at its highest since 2022, and Germany's storage barely half full weeks before winter. The strategic picture is now less about the headline war and more about its downstream consequences: an Atlantic basin losing access to crude it once took for granted, a product-fuel emergency in Europe, and Western capital pivoting toward non-chokepoint supply in Africa. The question going forward is whether emergency releases and market incentives can bridge the gap, or whether this autumn forces a deeper reckoning with Europe's dependence on corridors it no longer controls.
sources: Bloomberg, Reuters, OilPrice.com, TotalEnergies, Gas Infrastructure Europe (AGSI), ING, INES, Energy Intelligence
